titre: Baarle, Where a House Changes Countries Between the Living Room and the Entryway
accroche: Twenty-two Belgian enclaves lost in the Netherlands, eight Dutch enclaves nestled inside them: a medieval land deal never redrawn.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the Loveren, a street in Baarle, one house bears two numbers and two flags on its facade: No. 2, Belgian, and No. 19, Dutch, because the border runs straight through the threshold of the front door. This is not an isolated oddity: the municipality has twenty-two Belgian enclaves lost in Dutch territory, and eight Dutch enclaves nested inside some of them.

## The Mechanism

The origin goes back to land transactions long predating the existence of Belgium and the Netherlands as separate states: sales and exchanges concluded between the dukes of Brabant and the lords of Breda scattered plots there, cut off from one another, with no concern for territorial continuity, a division that was not really one as long as both blocks of land fell under neighboring sovereignties. It becomes one when Belgium breaks away from the Netherlands in 1830: each plot must now pick a side.

The Convention of Maastricht, signed on August 8, 1843 to delimit the Belgian-Dutch border, could have settled things with a stroke of the pen. It did not: at Baarle, lacking agreement on an overall boundary, the negotiators fell back on a cadastral survey of 1841, assigning each plot to Belgium or the Netherlands according to its historical lineage rather than any logic of continuous territory. The result: a border made of several thousand separate plots, rather than a line.

## The Shift

This 1843 compromise did not close the case for good. Two plots in the Zondereygen section, fourteen hectares in all, remained contested: an earlier municipal survey assigned them to the Netherlands, while the map annexed to the 1843 convention gave them to Belgium. The disagreement was settled only a century later, on June 20, 1959, by the International Court of Justice: the highest court in international law, called on to rule over fourteen hectares of fields. The Court found in favor of Belgium.

The patchwork, for its part, was never redrawn: it continues to govern daily life. The local rule is that the nationality of a house straddling the border is determined by the location of its front door: a principle that decides less the nationality of its residents than which country supplies their electricity, telephone service, or garbage collection. An ownership deal struck in the Middle Ages thus still decides, eight centuries later, which administration services an electrical wire on a street in Baarle.

repere.texte: On June 20, 1959, the International Court of Justice awards Belgium sovereignty over two plots at Baarle contested since 1843: fourteen hectares that two states were still disputing, more than a century after the treaty meant to fix their border.
repere.source: International Court of Justice, Case No. 38, “Sovereignty over Certain Frontier Land”

carte.punch: In Baarle, you can change countries just by walking through your front door.
carte.idee: Medieval land sales left 22 Belgian enclaves in Dutch territory, and 8 Dutch ones inside them. The 1843 treaty drew no border: it validated an old cadastral survey, plot by plot, and two of those plots ended up before the International Court of Justice.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Demarcating sovereignty: a history of Dutch-Belgian land swaps (OUPblog)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Academic analysis of the history of Belgian-Dutch territorial exchanges, including the episodes of 1648 and 1843.

quiz.question: Why did the 1843 boundary treaty between Belgium and the Netherlands not put an end to the territorial tangle of Baarle?
choix: Because the two countries refused to recognize a single shared village, for religious reasons
Because the border followed the course of a river that changed bed after the treaty was signed
Because no surveyor had been able to access the marshy area at the time the treaty was signed
Because it validated an old cadastral survey plot by plot, without drawing an overall border
quiz.explication: Rather than draw a continuous line, the 1843 negotiators assigned each plot to Belgium or the Netherlands according to an 1841 cadastral survey inherited from much earlier land sales and exchanges: this froze, rather than resolved, the fragmentation, to the point that an international court had to rule on the fate of two plots more than a century later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who supplies electricity, telephone service, or garbage collection to a house in Baarle that the border runs through?
choix: The administration of the country from which most of the street's residents originate
Both administrations in equal shares, under a municipal agreement signed in 1843
The administration of the country where the house's front door is located
The administration chosen by a vote of the household concerned
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The local rule makes public services depend on the location of the front door, not on the residents' nationality or on a negotiated split between administrations.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many hectares were at stake in the Zondereygen dispute settled by the International Court of Justice in 1959?
choix: About fourteen hectares, spread over two plots
About one hundred forty hectares, spread over twelve plots
About four hectares, a single contested plot
About forty hectares, shared among three municipalities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The dispute concerned plots 91 and 92 in the Zondereygen section, about fourteen hectares in all, contested since the 1843 convention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Baarle's fragmentation into dozens of enclaves come from?
choix: From a decision by Napoleon Bonaparte aimed at weakening the local landed nobility after 1810
From a religious partition following the Protestant Reformation in the Spanish Netherlands
From a border line drawn in haste during World War I
From land sales and exchanges between the dukes of Brabant and the lords of Breda, before Belgium existed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The fragmentation goes back to land transactions between the dukes of Brabant and the lords of Breda, concluded when the two territories still fell under neighboring sovereignties, not separate states.
